records.our_prose: A deliberate wildlife-gardening use. Ripening cones left standing feed American goldfinches and other seed-eating songbirds into fall and winter, functioning as a natural bird feeder; NC State suggests cutting dead stems only to 12 to 24 inches and letting them stand until they disintegrate. The tension is direct: leaving cones for birds is the opposite of deadheading for more bloom or a tidy look, so choose by intent, and it is also how the plant self-sows.

records.our_prose: The signature coneflower disease and the one to know: aster yellows is caused by a phytoplasma spread by leafhoppers (and can be carried on tools). Symptoms are diagnostic and bizarre: a witches broom in the flower head that resembles a small broccoli head, greening and deformation of the petals, stunting, and possible death. There is no cure and insecticides do not stop transmission. Rogue out and destroy infected plants promptly (do not compost them), disinfect pruners, and mow or clear weedy, grassy areas that harbor the leafhopper vectors.

records.our_prose: Coneflower rosette mites (Eriophyid mites) are microscopic and live inside developing flower buds, causing tufts of stunted, distorted flower parts and leaf-like growths erupting from the cone. Because they are shielded within the bud, contact miticides are largely ineffective. Management is cultural: prune out and destroy affected heads. This distortion is sometimes confused with aster yellows, but eriophyid damage is localized to individual heads rather than deforming the whole plant.

records.our_prose: Echinacea (purple coneflower) does well in the Las Vegas Valley: plant one division or transplant in spring in full sun and fast-draining soil, and it comes back every year, blooming from early summer into fall. Unlike bee balm and mint, it is drought-tolerant and does not need a summer break here; water deeply but infrequently and leave the seed heads standing for the birds.

records.source_context: It is native to the prairies of the Ozark region and central and southwestern Arkansas and is hardy in Zones 4 to 7. The yellow coneflower has drooping ray flowers that reach 3 to 6 inches wide. It is drought-tolerant and does not tolerate wet soil. Due to its poor tolerance for wet soil, it may not reliably overwinter in South Carolina.
